query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In HEA nanoparticles, the preservation of a single-phase solid solution across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges is governed by the interplay between high configurational entropy and local lattice distortions. The high entropy provides a thermodynamic driving force that favors mixing, while significant lattice distortions (arising from inherent differences in atomic radii and short-range ordering) create kinetic barriers that slow atomic diffusion. This combined effect maintains chemical and structural homogeneity up to high temperatures. However, if the local distortion is too weak, the thermal energy at elevated temperatures will overcome these kinetic barriers, leading to phase separation or elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near‐equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a single-phase solid solution with inherent lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA nanoparticles to controlled thermal cycles spanning 473–1923 K under inert or low‑oxygen atmospheres, with a controlled variable of lattice distortion (achieved by slight compositional adjustments that alter atomic size mismatches).
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in well‐controlled atmospheres (e.g., inert gas) to minimize extrinsic oxidation, with precise temperature control over the catalytic/thermoelectric range; a controlled comparison is made between HEA nanoparticles intentionally designed to have higher lattice distortions versus those with minimal distortion, keeping initial solid solution structure constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and any resultant short-range atomic ordering that increase diffusion activation barriers.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy favors a uniform mix by reducing the mixing enthalpy penalty; simultaneously, lattice distortions induce significant kinetic barriers by creating an energy landscape that hinders atomic diffusion. Together, these factors maintain the homogeneity of the solid solution during high-temperature operation. If the lattice distortion is insufficient, elevated temperatures will allow atomic rearrangements that lead to phase separation or chemical ordering.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with pronounced lattice distortions will remain largely as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with minimal elemental segregation even when thermally stressed up to 1923 K, while those with reduced lattice distortion will show measurable phase separation or local chemical ordering (e.g., elemental clustering or emergent secondary phases) at the upper end of the temperature range.
generation.baseline: The initial state is a homogenously mixed, single-phase HEA nanoparticle with a specific degree of inherent lattice distortion.
generation.boundary: This mechanism holds as long as the combination of high configurational entropy and kinetic stabilization via lattice distortions is sufficient to overcome the thermal activation of atomic diffusion. If the thermal energy exceeds the diffusion barriers—either by using nanoparticles with very low intrinsic lattice distortion or operating at temperatures beyond 1923 K—the stability mechanism may fail, leading to observable segregation or phase transformation.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty in the precise quantitative threshold at which thermal energy overcomes lattice distortion-induced kinetic barriers. This hypothesis extends findings from studies on entropy-stabilized diffusion (e.g., PMC7069714: stability of MEA-NPs) and the influence of lattice distortions on thermodynamic stability (e.g., PMC10983832: scaling laws for lattice distortions) into the regime of combined catalytic and thermoelectric operations. The temperature dependence of diffusion barriers and the role of minor elemental differences need further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles with identical nominal compositions and single-phase solid solution structures but differing in their induced lattice distortion: one set by selecting elements with moderately different atomic radii (yielding significant distortions) and a second set by choosing elements with very similar atomic sizes (minimizing distortions). Subject both sets to repeated thermal cycling over the 473–1923 K range under inert atmosphere and monitor their phase and chemical homogeneity in situ.
measurements: In situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for microstructural and compositional mapping
Time-resolved annealing studies to track the onset and progression of elemental segregation or phase transformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets maintain similar levels of phase purity and chemical homogeneity with no significant differences in the onset or extent of elemental segregation across the temperature range, then the role of local lattice distortions as a kinetic barrier is not supported. Alternatively, if the high-distortion samples unexpectedly degrade (i.e., show phase separation or chemical ordering earlier than the minimal distortion samples), the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. We demonstrate that the impact of this inter-atomic length disorder (representing static lattice distortion) and temperature fluctuations (representing dynamic lattice distortion) on fundamental and universal thermodynamic, structural, and elastic characteristics are similar and can be unified through effective temperature; i.e. a scaling law for HEAs that establishes a relationship between these factors. The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).
